securityTopics.commonMistake: Using one IP limit for every endpoint and blocking legitimate users behind shared networks.

securityTopics.question: How do you manage secrets across local, CI, and production environments?
securityTopics.coreAnswer: Keep secrets out of source and images, inject them at runtime from an approved store, restrict access, rotate credentials, and prevent values from entering logs or client bundles.
securityTopics.example: The backend receives an email provider key at runtime, while the Vite frontend receives only explicitly public configuration and never the private credential.
securityTopics.commonMistake: Using an environment file but committing it or exposing a private key through a public frontend prefix.

securityTopics.question: How do you secure file uploads?
securityTopics.coreAnswer: Authenticate and authorize the upload, limit size and type, verify content rather than trusting the filename, use generated object names, scan when risk requires it, and serve from isolated storage.
securityTopics.example: A résumé upload uses a short-lived presigned URL, validates the final object, stores it outside the application server, and never executes uploaded content.
securityTopics.commonMistake: Accepting an extension as proof of file type or placing uploads under an executable web root.

securityTopics.question: How do you use the OWASP Top 10 in everyday engineering?
securityTopics.coreAnswer: Use it as a risk checklist during design and review, then translate each relevant risk into concrete controls, automated checks, and ownership for the product's actual attack surface.
securityTopics.example: For a project inquiry form, cover injection, abuse, sensitive-data logging, dependency risk, rate limits, server-side validation, and least-privilege email credentials.
securityTopics.commonMistake: Memorizing vulnerability names without explaining how the architecture prevents or detects them.

securityDiagramScenarios.title: Protecting a public form with defense in depth
securityDiagramScenarios.question: How would you stop spam, injection, and stored attacks on a public contact or application form?
securityDiagramScenarios.coreAnswer: Treat every browser value as untrusted. Keep client validation for usability, then enforce server-side schema validation, abuse controls, safe database access, context-aware output handling, and monitoring at separate trust boundaries.
securityDiagramScenarios.seniorFraming: No single control prevents every attack. A honeypot reduces simple bot noise, but it does not replace rate limiting, server validation, parameterized queries, authorization, encoding, or alerting.

flows.label: Design A: direct trust path

nodes.title: Public browser
nodes.detail: Attacker can bypass JavaScript checks.

nodes.title: Form endpoint
nodes.detail: Accepts fields and sends or stores them directly.

nodes.title: Email or database
nodes.detail: Receives unchecked content and repeated requests.

flows.note: This design trusts the client and gives one endpoint responsibility for validation, abuse prevention, persistence, and detection.

flows.label: Design B: layered request path

nodes.title: Browser
nodes.detail: UX validation and an invisible honeypot field.

nodes.title: CDN and WAF
nodes.detail: Blocks known abusive traffic before the app.

nodes.title: Rate limit and bot check
nodes.detail: Controls bursts and challenges suspicious requests.

nodes.title: Server validation
nodes.detail: Allowlisted schema, length, type, and business rules.

nodes.title: Safe processing
nodes.detail: Parameterized access, encoded output, and monitored delivery.

flows.note: Each layer has a narrow job. If a simple bot bypasses the honeypot, later controls still protect capacity and data.

steps.title: Reduce automated noise
steps.detail: Use a visually hidden honeypot that real users leave empty, minimum-submit-time checks, and a privacy-conscious challenge such as Turnstile when traffic looks suspicious.

steps.title: Control request volume
steps.detail: Rate limit at the edge and application by route cost, IP, account, and tenant where appropriate. Return HTTP 429 with Retry-After rather than silently dropping legitimate traffic.

steps.title: Validate on the server
steps.detail: Parse against an allowlisted schema before business logic. Enforce required fields, types, lengths, ranges, formats, and cross-field rules; client checks are only an early UX aid.

steps.title: Handle data for its destination
steps.detail: Use parameterized queries or an ORM for SQL, encode output for its HTML, attribute, URL, or JavaScript context, and sanitize only when users are intentionally allowed to author HTML.

steps.title: Protect state and identity
steps.detail: Use CSRF protection for cookie-authenticated writes, authorize every protected operation, keep secrets server-side, and use least-privilege credentials for email or storage services.

steps.title: Observe and respond
steps.detail: Record validation failures, blocked bursts, delivery failures, and unusual patterns without logging passwords, tokens, or sensitive message content. Alert on sustained abuse.

securityDiagramScenarios.interviewAnswer: I would protect the form in layers: an optional honeypot and timing signal for simple bots, edge and route-level rate limits for abuse, authoritative server-side schema validation, parameterized persistence, and context-aware encoding when data is shown again. Rich HTML is the exception that needs a maintained sanitizer. I would also add CSRF protection where cookies authenticate writes and monitor blocked and failed requests so the controls can be tuned.
securityDiagramScenarios.commonMistake: Calling validation, sanitization, and encoding the same thing. Validation decides whether input is allowed; sanitization removes unsafe markup when markup is permitted; encoding keeps data from becoming executable in a specific output context.

securityDiagramScenarios.title: HTTP vs HTTPS and the TLS trust path
securityDiagramScenarios.question: What does HTTPS actually protect, and what security work remains after enabling it?
securityDiagramScenarios.coreAnswer: HTTP sends application traffic without transport encryption. HTTPS is HTTP carried through TLS, which authenticates the server certificate and protects data confidentiality and integrity while it travels between TLS endpoints.
securityDiagramScenarios.seniorFraming: HTTPS protects data in transit, not the application itself. It does not replace authentication, authorization, input validation, secure sessions, safe database access, output encoding, or encryption at rest.

flows.label: Design A: plain HTTP request

nodes.title: Browser
nodes.detail: Sends URLs, headers, cookies, and form data as plain transport traffic.

nodes.title: Public network
nodes.detail: A network observer may read or alter the request and response.

nodes.title: Application server
nodes.detail: Cannot prove that transport content arrived without interception or modification.

flows.note: HTTP may be acceptable inside a tightly controlled local boundary, but public user traffic and credentials should never rely on an unencrypted path.

flows.label: Design B: HTTPS with TLS

nodes.title: Browser
nodes.detail: Requests a secure connection and validates the server identity.

nodes.title: Certificate and handshake
nodes.detail: TLS negotiates keys after the certificate chain and hostname are checked.

nodes.title: Encrypted channel
nodes.detail: Authenticated encryption protects confidentiality and detects tampering in transit.

nodes.title: TLS endpoint
nodes.detail: The CDN, load balancer, or app decrypts traffic and continues normal application security checks.

flows.note: If TLS terminates at a CDN or load balancer, decide whether internal hops also need TLS based on trust boundaries, network exposure, and compliance requirements.

controlMappings.controls: Traffic can be read in transit
controlMappings.explanation: TLS encrypts traffic between its endpoints.

controlMappings.controls: Traffic can be modified without reliable detection

controlMappings.explanation: The client validates the certificate chain and requested hostname.
Still requires secure application code; HTTPS only protects the transport layer.

steps.title: Start the TLS handshake
steps.detail: The client and server agree on a supported TLS version and cryptographic parameters.

steps.title: Verify server identity
steps.detail: The client checks the certificate authority chain, expiration, hostname, and certificate validity before trusting the endpoint.

steps.title: Establish session keys
steps.detail: The handshake derives short-lived symmetric keys so application traffic can be encrypted efficiently.

steps.title: Exchange protected HTTP
steps.detail: Requests and responses remain normal HTTP semantics, but TLS encrypts and authenticates their bytes in transit.

steps.title: Continue application controls
steps.detail: The server still authenticates users, authorizes actions, validates payloads, protects sessions, and safely handles stored and rendered data.

securityDiagramScenarios.interviewAnswer: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS. TLS authenticates the server and protects confidentiality and integrity between TLS endpoints. I would terminate it at the edge or load balancer, use managed certificate rotation, redirect HTTP to HTTPS, enable HSTS after confirming every route supports HTTPS, and use Secure cookies. I would still enforce all application-level controls because TLS does not prevent injection, broken authorization, or compromised accounts.
securityDiagramScenarios.commonMistake: Saying HTTPS encrypts the database or makes the application secure. It protects transport between TLS endpoints; stored data and application behavior need separate controls.

securityDiagramScenarios.title: Security concepts that sound similar but solve different problems
securityDiagramScenarios.question: How do authentication, authorization, hashing, encryption, validation, sanitization, encoding, CORS, and CSRF fit together?
securityDiagramScenarios.coreAnswer: Define each control by the question it answers and place it at the correct trust boundary. Similar terms are not interchangeable, and using the wrong one often leaves the actual exploit condition untouched.
securityDiagramScenarios.seniorFraming: A strong answer explains sequence and ownership: identify the caller, decide permission, validate the request, process and store safely, then encode or sanitize for the output context while recording security-relevant events.

flows.label: Secure request decision path

nodes.title: Authenticate
nodes.detail: Who is making this request?

nodes.title: Authorize
nodes.detail: May this identity perform this action on this resource?

nodes.title: Validate
nodes.detail: Does the payload match allowed types, bounds, formats, and business rules?

nodes.title: Process safely
nodes.detail: Use parameterized persistence, least privilege, and explicit domain rules.

nodes.title: Render safely
nodes.detail: Encode for the output context or sanitize intentionally allowed HTML.

flows.note: The order matters, but every boundary still fails closed. Validation does not grant permission, and authorization does not make unsafe output safe.

controlMappings.explanation: A valid session identifies Mico; an ownership or role check decides whether Mico can edit a specific project.

controlMappings.controls: One-way fingerprint vs reversible secrecy vs format conversion
controlMappings.explanation: Hash passwords with Argon2; encrypt sensitive recoverable data with managed keys; Base64 only converts bytes and provides no secrecy.

controlMappings.threat: Validation vs sanitization vs output encoding
controlMappings.controls: Accept allowed input vs clean permitted markup vs render data safely
controlMappings.explanation: Reject an invalid email, sanitize user-authored rich HTML, and HTML-encode plain comments when displaying them.

controlMappings.controls: Browser response-sharing policy vs forged authenticated request defense
controlMappings.explanation: CORS controls which origins may read responses; CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies protect cookie-authenticated state changes.

controlMappings.controls: Edge filtering vs authoritative domain rules
controlMappings.explanation: A WAF blocks known malicious patterns; the application still validates every field and enforces business invariants.

controlMappings.controls: Trap simple bots vs bound request volume
controlMappings.explanation: A hidden field catches basic scripts; rate limits still protect resources when sophisticated bots ignore the trap.

steps.title: Ask what is being protected
steps.detail: Clarify whether the concern is identity, permission, transport, stored data, input correctness, browser rendering, or service capacity.

steps.title: Choose the control that removes the exploit condition
steps.detail: Use authorization for object access, parameterization for SQL injection, contextual encoding for rendered text, and rate limiting for resource abuse.

steps.title: Place it at the authoritative boundary
steps.detail: Client-side checks improve usability, but security decisions belong on the server or another trusted enforcement point.

steps.title: Add supporting layers
steps.detail: Use edge filtering, monitoring, alerts, least privilege, and recovery controls without confusing them for the primary defense.

steps.title: Test the negative path
steps.detail: Try missing permissions, cross-tenant IDs, malformed values, unsafe markup, reused credentials, forged origins, and repeated requests.

securityDiagramScenarios.interviewAnswer: I separate these terms by purpose. Authentication proves identity and authorization checks permission. Hashing is one-way and fits passwords, encryption is reversible with a key, and encoding is only representation. Validation rejects disallowed input, sanitization cleans intentionally supported markup, and output encoding prevents plain data from becoming executable. CORS controls browser response sharing, while CSRF defenses protect cookie-authenticated writes. I apply each at its authoritative boundary and then add monitoring and rate limits as supporting layers.
securityDiagramScenarios.commonMistake: Using one security term as a substitute for another, such as Base64 encoding a secret, relying on CORS to stop CSRF, or assuming a validated value is authorized and safe in every output context.

securityDiagramScenarios.title: Matching attacks to the correct controls
securityDiagramScenarios.question: Which protection would you choose for each common web attack, and why is one generic security filter not enough?
securityDiagramScenarios.coreAnswer: Start with the attacker's path and the asset at risk, then place preventive, detective, and recovery controls at the relevant boundary. Different attacks exploit different assumptions, so the controls must be specific.
securityDiagramScenarios.seniorFraming: Name the primary control first, then the supporting layers and remaining risk. For example, CSP can limit XSS impact, but correct rendering and sanitization remain the primary defenses.

controlMappings.explanation: A honeypot catches simple automation; behavioral limits and edge challenges handle bots that behave more like browsers.

controlMappings.controls: Schema validation, ORM or parameterized queries
controlMappings.explanation: Validation rejects invalid values, while parameterization prevents data from becoming part of the SQL command.

controlMappings.controls: Safe rendering, contextual encoding, HTML sanitization, CSP
controlMappings.explanation: Keep untrusted data out of executable contexts; sanitize only intentionally supported HTML and use CSP as containment.

controlMappings.controls: SameSite cookies, CSRF token, Origin checks
controlMappings.explanation: Prove that a cookie-authenticated state-changing request came through an intended application flow.

controlMappings.controls: Rate limit, MFA or passkeys, breached-password screening
controlMappings.explanation: Slow automated credential replay and reduce the value of a reused password without locking out every shared-network user.

controlMappings.controls: CDN, WAF, edge limits, load shedding
controlMappings.explanation: Absorb or reject abusive traffic before scarce application and database capacity is consumed.

steps.title: Identify the asset
steps.detail: Clarify whether the risk is account access, private data, service capacity, stored content, money, or administrative control.

steps.title: Trace the trust boundaries
steps.detail: Follow the request through browser, edge, API, queue, worker, database, and third-party services. Mark where identity or data assumptions change.

steps.title: Choose the primary control
steps.detail: Use the control that removes the exploit condition: parameterization for SQL injection, authorization for object access, or safe rendering for XSS.

steps.title: Add supporting layers
steps.detail: Add limits, monitoring, containment, and recovery so one bypass or operational failure does not become a complete compromise.

steps.title: Test the abuse case
steps.detail: Verify negative paths such as cross-tenant IDs, repeated login attempts, malformed payloads, unsafe HTML, missing CSRF tokens, and oversized files.

securityDiagramScenarios.interviewAnswer: I avoid prescribing one security middleware for every risk. I identify the asset, trace the trust boundary, and choose the primary control that removes the exploit condition. Then I add rate limits, monitoring, and containment around it. For SQL injection that means parameterized access; for XSS it means safe sinks and context-aware encoding; for credential stuffing it means rate limits plus stronger authentication.
securityDiagramScenarios.commonMistake: Listing security products without connecting each one to an attack path, a protected asset, and a remaining trade-off.

securityDiagramScenarios.title: Responding when an API may be under attack
securityDiagramScenarios.question: Traffic, errors, and suspicious requests suddenly spike. How do you protect users without destroying the evidence you need?
securityDiagramScenarios.coreAnswer: Confirm the signal, contain the active risk at the narrowest effective boundary, preserve evidence, remove the exploit or abused credential, restore safely, and turn the incident into durable controls.
securityDiagramScenarios.seniorFraming: Availability and security are connected. Scaling can buy investigation time, but scaling a vulnerable endpoint may increase cost or blast radius; containment and evidence come before an unproven capacity change.

flows.label: Incident response sequence

nodes.title: Detect
nodes.detail: Correlate rate, latency, errors, identities, routes, and logs.

nodes.title: Contain
nodes.detail: Block, limit, revoke, isolate, or disable the abused path.

nodes.title: Preserve evidence
nodes.detail: Keep relevant logs, timestamps, request IDs, and configuration snapshots.

nodes.title: Fix and recover
nodes.detail: Patch the cause, rotate secrets, verify data, and restore gradually.

nodes.title: Learn
nodes.detail: Document timeline, root cause, missed signals, and owned actions.

flows.note: Containment should be reversible and scoped when possible. Preserve enough evidence to understand whether the event was abuse, exploitation, or a normal traffic surge.

steps.title: Confirm and classify
steps.detail: Compare current traffic with baseline, identify affected routes and tenants, inspect status codes and payload shapes, and distinguish legitimate demand from automation or exploitation.

steps.title: Limit blast radius
steps.detail: Apply an emergency edge rule, route-specific limit, account lock, feature kill switch, or temporary read-only mode. Avoid taking the entire product offline if one path can be isolated.

steps.title: Preserve evidence
steps.detail: Retain logs, traces, request IDs, deployment versions, security events, and relevant database audit history. Restrict access and avoid modifying originals needed for investigation.

steps.title: Remove the cause
steps.detail: Patch vulnerable code or configuration, revoke sessions or credentials, rotate exposed secrets, close excessive permissions, and validate whether data was read or changed.

steps.title: Recover gradually
steps.detail: Restore traffic in stages, monitor saturation and security signals, verify user-critical paths, and keep rollback or containment controls ready.

steps.title: Run a blameless review
steps.detail: Create the timeline, root cause, impact, detection gaps, and prioritized actions with owners and dates. Update runbooks, alerts, tests, and architecture where needed.

securityDiagramScenarios.interviewAnswer: I would first confirm whether the spike is legitimate demand, automated abuse, or exploitation by correlating routes, identities, errors, latency, and recent changes. I would contain the narrowest risky path at the edge or application, preserve logs and request evidence, then patch or revoke the root cause. Recovery would be gradual with security and reliability signals watched together, followed by a blameless review with owned actions.
securityDiagramScenarios.commonMistake: Immediately adding servers or deleting suspicious logs. More capacity does not remove a vulnerability, and lost evidence makes root-cause and impact analysis harder.

items.question: How do you decide where state belongs?
items.coreAnswer: Keep state at the lowest shared owner, derive values instead of duplicating them, and separate server state, URL state, form state, and ephemeral UI state.
items.example: In a map product, the URL can own shareable address and radius filters, TanStack Query can own fetched establishments, and local state can own an open popover.
items.commonMistake: Putting all state into one global store because it is available.

items.question: What causes a React component to re-render?
items.coreAnswer: A component re-renders when its state changes, its parent renders, consumed context changes, or an external subscription updates.
items.example: Profile first. Split frequently changing context, stabilize expensive list inputs, and virtualize large collections instead of adding memoization everywhere.
items.commonMistake: Assuming every render is a performance bug.

items.question: How would you design a reusable component API?
items.coreAnswer: Start from semantic HTML and user tasks, expose a small controlled surface, support composition, and avoid leaking implementation details.
items.example: A modal exposes open, onOpenChange, title, description, and children while owning focus trap, Escape handling, and scroll lock.
items.commonMistake: Building one component with dozens of styling and behavior flags.

items.question: How do you improve React performance?
items.coreAnswer: Measure the user-visible bottleneck, reduce unnecessary work, improve loading strategy, and verify the result with profiling and Web Vitals.
items.example: For a dense dashboard, split the route bundle, virtualize long tables, defer non-critical charts, and keep interactions responsive before optimizing micro-renders.
items.commonMistake: Starting with useMemo before checking network, bundle, rendering, or layout cost.

items.question: When should you use useEffect?
items.coreAnswer: Use an effect to synchronize React with an external system, not to derive values that can be calculated during rendering or handled in an event.
items.example: Subscribe to a map instance or browser API in an effect and clean it up. Derive a filtered project list directly from props and state instead of copying it into effect-managed state.
items.commonMistake: Using effects as a general-purpose reaction system and creating loops or stale state.

items.question: How do you choose client rendering, SSR, and static generation in React applications?
items.coreAnswer: Choose per route based on indexability, personalization, data freshness, interactivity, and operational complexity.
items.example: A public project article can be statically generated, a search landing page may use SSR, and an authenticated operations dashboard can primarily render on the client.
items.commonMistake: Equating SSR with automatic performance or SEO regardless of the route.

items.question: How do you make large React lists responsive?
items.coreAnswer: Reduce the data and DOM work first, then use stable keys, pagination or incremental loading, and virtualization when the visible window is much smaller than the dataset.
items.example: For a live order feed, paginate historical orders, keep active orders bounded, and virtualize long history instead of rendering thousands of rows.
items.commonMistake: Virtualizing a small list while ignoring an oversized network response or expensive row component.

items.question: When do you use computed, watch, and methods?
items.coreAnswer: Use computed for cached derived values, watch for side effects caused by reactive changes, and methods for explicit actions.
items.example: A selected radius label is computed; changing radius may trigger a watched fetch; clicking Reset is a method.
items.commonMistake: Using watchers to maintain state that could be derived.

items.question: How do you choose SSR, SSG, and client rendering in Nuxt?
items.coreAnswer: Choose per route based on freshness, personalization, indexability, and infrastructure cost.
items.example: Clinic pages benefit from SSR or prerendering for SEO, while an authenticated analytics dashboard can render mostly on the client.
items.commonMistake: Choosing one rendering mode for the entire product without considering route needs.

items.question: How do you structure reusable Vue logic?
items.coreAnswer: Use focused composables for reusable stateful behavior and keep domain rules separate from visual components.
items.example: useNeighborhoodSearch can own query parameters, request cancellation, loading, and normalization while map and compare views consume the same contract.
items.commonMistake: Creating a universal composable that mixes API, UI, routing, and business rules.

items.question: How do you prevent hydration mismatch?
items.coreAnswer: Make server and first client render deterministic, defer browser-only values, and isolate client-only libraries.
items.example: Do not render Date.now, window dimensions, or localStorage-derived content differently during hydration; initialize them after mount or serialize stable server state.
items.commonMistake: Suppressing the warning without fixing divergent output.

items.question: What is the difference between ref and reactive?
items.coreAnswer: ref wraps a value behind .value in JavaScript and works well for primitives or replaceable objects; reactive creates a proxy for an object whose identity is expected to remain stable.
items.example: Use a ref for selectedRadius and a reactive object for a cohesive edit form, while avoiding destructuring reactive properties without toRefs.
items.commonMistake: Choosing based only on shorter syntax and losing reactivity through destructuring.

items.question: How do useAsyncData and useFetch fit into Nuxt data loading?
items.coreAnswer: Use Nuxt data utilities when data should participate in SSR, payload serialization, caching, and route-aware loading; keep client-only requests explicit.
items.example: Load indexable clinic data with useAsyncData on the server, while a user-triggered export can call $fetch from an event because it is not part of initial rendering.
items.commonMistake: Fetching the same initial data again after hydration because server payload reuse was ignored.

items.question: How do you improve performance in a large Vue application?
items.coreAnswer: Measure first, reduce reactive and rendering scope, split route code, avoid unnecessary deep reactivity, and keep large collections bounded.
items.example: Keep a third-party map instance in a shallowRef, lazy-load analytics routes, and send clustered map data instead of making thousands of deeply reactive marker objects.
items.commonMistake: Adding watchers and computed layers without understanding which reactive dependency triggers the work.

agileDeliveryTopics.question: How do Agile, Waterfall, Scrum, and Kanban differ?
agileDeliveryTopics.coreAnswer: Agile is a set of principles built around incremental delivery, feedback, and adaptation. Waterfall moves through defined phases with most scope and sequencing planned up front. Scrum is an Agile framework that uses fixed-length sprints, accountabilities, events, and artifacts. Kanban manages continuous flow through visible work and work-in-progress limits.
agileDeliveryTopics.example: A product team can use Scrum to deliver DineEase capabilities in two-week increments. A support team can use Kanban because work arrives continuously. A compliance-heavy migration with fixed approvals may use Waterfall-style gates while still validating risky assumptions early.
agileDeliveryTopics.commonMistake: Treating Agile as no planning, Waterfall as automatically bad, Scrum as a synonym for Agile, or Kanban as only a board with columns.

agileDeliveryTopics.question: When would you choose Waterfall, Scrum, Kanban, or a hybrid approach?
agileDeliveryTopics.coreAnswer: Choose from the uncertainty and flow of work. Waterfall fits stable scope with sequential approvals, Scrum fits complex product work that benefits from a regular inspect-and-adapt cadence, Kanban fits continuous or unpredictable demand, and a hybrid approach fits organizations with fixed governance but iterative implementation.
agileDeliveryTopics.example: A healthcare integration may require formal security and compliance gates, but the application can still be built and validated in small Scrum increments. Production support can run through a Kanban lane with explicit service classes and work-in-progress limits.
agileDeliveryTopics.commonMistake: Choosing a framework because it is popular instead of matching it to requirement stability, delivery risk, team ownership, and how work actually arrives.

agileDeliveryTopics.question: How do you become an effective Scrum Master?
agileDeliveryTopics.coreAnswer: Learn Scrum deeply, facilitate rather than command, protect transparency, coach the team toward self-management, help remove impediments, improve collaboration with the Product Owner, and use evidence to make the delivery system better. The Scrum Master owns the effectiveness of Scrum, not the assignment of tasks.
agileDeliveryTopics.example: Start by making the sprint goal and blockers visible. Facilitate planning, daily Scrum, review, and retrospective around their purpose, not a script. If reviews are slow, help the team agree on smaller pull requests and a review window, then inspect whether cycle time improves. Coach the team to own the change rather than assigning the solution yourself.
agileDeliveryTopics.commonMistake: Acting as a project manager who assigns tickets, runs status meetings, shields the team from all accountability, or measures success only through velocity.

agileDeliveryTopics.question: What should a Scrum Master do during each Scrum event?
agileDeliveryTopics.coreAnswer: Ensure each event has a clear purpose, the right participants, useful preparation, healthy facilitation, and an outcome the team understands. Step in when the process is unclear, but allow the Developers and Product Owner to own their decisions.
agileDeliveryTopics.example: In planning, help the team form one sprint goal and select coherent work. In the daily Scrum, keep focus on progress toward that goal rather than reporting to a manager. In review, gather stakeholder feedback on the increment. In retrospective, leave with one or two owned improvements and inspect them next sprint.
agileDeliveryTopics.commonMistake: Becoming the permanent meeting chair and note taker instead of teaching the team to facilitate, inspect, and adapt for itself.

agileDeliveryTopics.question: What should happen during sprint planning?
agileDeliveryTopics.coreAnswer: Agree on a meaningful sprint goal, review priority and capacity, expose dependencies and risks, then select work that forms a coherent achievable increment.
agileDeliveryTopics.example: For a DineEase ordering milestone, the goal might be a reliable dine-in order flow. Menu editing that is required for that flow belongs in scope; unrelated analytics polish does not.
agileDeliveryTopics.commonMistake: Filling capacity with unrelated tickets and calling the resulting list a sprint commitment.

agileDeliveryTopics.question: How do you estimate technical work?
agileDeliveryTopics.coreAnswer: Break work into understood slices, identify uncertainty and dependencies, compare complexity with known work, and communicate a confidence range rather than pretending an estimate is certainty.
agileDeliveryTopics.example: Before estimating a kiosk integration, run a short spike on the hardware and payment boundary, then estimate the user flow separately from the uncertain integration work.
agileDeliveryTopics.commonMistake: Converting story points directly into hours or hiding uncertainty inside a larger number.

agileDeliveryTopics.question: What do you do when the sprint goal is no longer achievable?
agileDeliveryTopics.coreAnswer: Raise the risk early, identify the blocker and user impact, present scope or sequencing options, and renegotiate work with the product owner while protecting quality and transparency.
agileDeliveryTopics.example: If a payment provider delays approval, complete the order state model and test integration while moving live payment activation to the next release instead of pretending the dependency is resolved.
agileDeliveryTopics.commonMistake: Waiting until the sprint review to reveal that the main outcome was never achievable.

agileDeliveryTopics.question: How do you handle a requirement change in the middle of a sprint?
agileDeliveryTopics.coreAnswer: Evaluate urgency and impact against the sprint goal. If it must enter, make the trade explicit by removing or rescheduling equivalent scope rather than silently overloading the team.
agileDeliveryTopics.example: A legal compliance fix may interrupt planned work; a lower-priority report leaves the sprint and stakeholders receive the revised expectation.
agileDeliveryTopics.commonMistake: Treating every stakeholder request as an emergency or saying Scrum forbids all change.

agileDeliveryTopics.question: What makes a retrospective useful?
agileDeliveryTopics.coreAnswer: Create psychological safety, discuss specific system and process evidence, choose one or two owned improvements, and review whether previous actions changed the outcome.
agileDeliveryTopics.example: If reviews repeatedly arrive late, agree on smaller pull requests and a daily review window, assign ownership, then inspect review lead time in the next retrospective.
agileDeliveryTopics.commonMistake: Repeating generic start-stop-continue comments without accountable follow-through.

agileDeliveryTopics.question: How do you manage technical debt in an Agile product team?
agileDeliveryTopics.coreAnswer: Describe debt through delivery, reliability, security, or user cost; rank it alongside product risk; and attach focused improvement to related feature work when possible.
agileDeliveryTopics.example: If duplicated order validation causes repeated defects, consolidate it as part of the next order workflow instead of requesting an unbounded rewrite sprint.
agileDeliveryTopics.commonMistake: Using technical debt as a label for any code an engineer dislikes.

agileDeliveryTopics.question: How do you resolve disagreement with product or design?
agileDeliveryTopics.coreAnswer: Return to the user and business objective, make constraints and evidence visible, propose options with consequences, and document the decision after the responsible owner chooses.
agileDeliveryTopics.example: If a requested animation threatens performance, demonstrate the measured cost and offer a lighter interaction that preserves the intended hierarchy and brand effect.
agileDeliveryTopics.commonMistake: Arguing from title, preference, or technical purity instead of shared outcomes.

agileDeliveryTopics.question: How do you lead delivery without being the formal manager?
agileDeliveryTopics.coreAnswer: Create clarity, expose dependencies, document decisions, unblock teammates, improve review quality, and make ownership visible without centralizing every decision around yourself.
agileDeliveryTopics.example: At ASTA, align frontend, backend, and product boundaries, give owners clear outcomes, and stay available for architectural decisions while allowing each engineer to own implementation.
agileDeliveryTopics.commonMistake: Becoming the approval bottleneck and calling it leadership.

leadershipTopics.question: How do you handle technical disagreement?
leadershipTopics.coreAnswer: Align on the decision criteria, make assumptions and trade-offs visible, time-box investigation, and document the decision.
leadershipTopics.example: If one engineer wants GraphQL and another wants REST, compare client data needs, team familiarity, caching, schema ownership, and operational cost before choosing.

leadershipTopics.question: How do you balance quality and delivery speed?
leadershipTopics.coreAnswer: Protect irreversible and high-risk quality while reducing scope, sequencing improvements, and making accepted debt explicit.
leadershipTopics.example: For a launch, preserve accessibility, data integrity, security, and observability. Defer a lower-value animation or secondary workflow with a clear follow-up owner.

leadershipTopics.question: How do you help engineers grow?
leadershipTopics.coreAnswer: Give context and ownership, calibrate support, review reasoning instead of style preferences, and create feedback loops.
leadershipTopics.example: Delegate a bounded feature with its success criteria and architecture context, then use design and code review to discuss trade-offs rather than taking the work back.

leadershipTopics.question: How do you lead an ambiguous project?
leadershipTopics.coreAnswer: Turn uncertainty into explicit assumptions, risks, milestones, decision owners, and thin end-to-end slices.
leadershipTopics.example: For DineEase, establish order and menu domain contracts first, deliver one restaurant workflow end to end, then expand to kiosk, analytics, and workforce surfaces.

leadershipTopics.question: Tell me about a production incident you led.
leadershipTopics.coreAnswer: Stabilize user impact first, establish one incident channel and owner, communicate clearly, preserve evidence, then follow with a blameless review and tracked actions.
leadershipTopics.example: If order updates stop reaching kitchen displays, fall back to API refresh, pause risky releases, inspect the delivery path, and communicate status. After recovery, document the trigger, detection gap, and prevention work.

leadershipTopics.question: How do you manage technical debt?
leadershipTopics.coreAnswer: Describe debt as a measurable delivery or reliability cost, rank it against product risk, and address it incrementally alongside feature work.
leadershipTopics.example: If duplicated order rules cause regressions across kiosk and dashboard surfaces, move the rule behind one domain contract as part of the next related feature rather than proposing an unbounded rewrite.

leadershipTopics.question: What do you do when a project will miss its deadline?
leadershipTopics.coreAnswer: Surface the risk early, separate fixed constraints from negotiable scope, present options with consequences, and protect the quality floor.
leadershipTopics.example: Keep the reliable core ordering workflow for launch, defer a secondary analytics view, document the follow-up, and avoid hiding schedule risk until the final week.

aiTopics.question: Where should AI fit in a product architecture?
aiTopics.coreAnswer: Use AI for probabilistic interpretation or generation, keep deterministic business rules outside the model, and validate outputs before side effects.
aiTopics.example: Automated menu setup can extract candidate items and modifiers, but a deterministic schema validator and user review must approve changes before publishing.

aiTopics.question: How do you make an AI feature reliable?
aiTopics.coreAnswer: Define eval cases, constrain output, version prompts and models, track latency and cost, and provide fallback and human review paths.
aiTopics.example: Test menu extraction against known documents, measure field accuracy, retry only transient failures, and preserve the source text for audit.

aiTopics.question: How do you protect an AI workflow?
aiTopics.coreAnswer: Treat model input and output as untrusted, restrict tools, minimize sensitive data, and require authorization at the action boundary.
aiTopics.example: A support assistant may draft a reply, but it cannot read another tenant’s data or send messages without the same authorization checks as a normal API request.

aiTopics.question: When would you use RAG instead of fine-tuning?
aiTopics.coreAnswer: Use retrieval-augmented generation when answers need current or private source material and citations; use fine-tuning mainly to change repeatable behavior, style, or task performance rather than to store frequently changing facts.
aiTopics.example: An ASTA knowledge assistant can retrieve current project and service documents at request time, while a fine-tuned model would be considered only if prompt examples cannot consistently produce the required response format or behavior.

aiTopics.question: How do you evaluate an AI feature before launch?
aiTopics.coreAnswer: Define representative test cases and failure categories, establish deterministic checks where possible, add human scoring for subjective quality, and compare versions against a baseline.
aiTopics.example: For menu extraction, score item, price, modifier, and category accuracy separately; track invalid schema output and measure how often a reviewer must correct the result.

aiTopics.question: How do you control AI latency and cost?
aiTopics.coreAnswer: Route work to the smallest adequate model, reduce unnecessary context, cache safe repeated results, batch asynchronous work, stream when useful, and enforce budgets and timeouts.
aiTopics.example: Interactive suggestions use a fast model and stream output, while a large menu import runs asynchronously with progress updates and a per-job token budget.

productThinkingTopics.question: How do you determine whether a feature was successful?
productThinkingTopics.coreAnswer: Define the user behavior and business outcome before building, establish a baseline and guardrails, then compare quantitative signals with qualitative feedback after release.
productThinkingTopics.example: For clinic discovery, measure successful clinic selection and booking starts while guarding search latency, accessibility, and irrelevant-result rates.
productThinkingTopics.commonMistake: Using page views or shipping completion as the only definition of success.

productThinkingTopics.question: How do you challenge a feature request constructively?
productThinkingTopics.coreAnswer: Clarify the underlying problem and evidence, identify constraints, then offer the smallest option that can test the assumption without dismissing the stakeholder's goal.
productThinkingTopics.example: Instead of immediately building a complex restaurant report, ask which decision it should support and test whether a smaller comparison view answers that question.
productThinkingTopics.commonMistake: Saying no based only on implementation effort or accepting a solution without understanding the problem.

productThinkingTopics.question: How do you turn an unclear business problem into technical scope?
productThinkingTopics.coreAnswer: Identify actors, desired outcomes, current workflow, constraints, data, exceptions, and success measures; then propose a thin end-to-end slice with explicit assumptions.
productThinkingTopics.example: For automated menu setup, map upload, extraction, review, correction, and publishing before deciding which AI model or queue technology to use.
productThinkingTopics.commonMistake: Starting with screens or a preferred stack before the workflow and decision boundaries are understood.

productThinkingTopics.question: How do you prioritize usability, performance, SEO, and delivery speed?
productThinkingTopics.coreAnswer: Set a non-negotiable quality floor, connect each concern to the route's user and business purpose, then sequence improvements according to measured risk and expected value.
productThinkingTopics.example: A public clinic page prioritizes indexability, performance, and accessible booking; an internal dashboard may prioritize interaction speed and operational clarity over public SEO.
productThinkingTopics.commonMistake: Applying the same optimization priorities to every route.

productThinkingTopics.question: How do you communicate technical trade-offs to non-engineers?
productThinkingTopics.coreAnswer: Explain choices through user impact, cost, risk, timing, and reversibility; present concrete options and a recommendation without hiding behind implementation jargon.
productThinkingTopics.example: Describe a queue as a way to keep imports responsive and recoverable, then explain the added operational cost and why synchronous processing becomes risky at expected volume.
productThinkingTopics.commonMistake: Giving a technical lecture instead of helping the stakeholder make a decision.

productThinkingTopics.question: How do you decide whether to build or buy?
productThinkingTopics.coreAnswer: Compare strategic differentiation, total ownership cost, integration effort, security, compliance, reliability, vendor lock-in, and exit options—not only subscription price.
productThinkingTopics.example: Use a proven email provider rather than operate mail delivery, but keep product-specific restaurant workflows in-house because they differentiate DineEase.
productThinkingTopics.commonMistake: Building commodity infrastructure for control or buying a core differentiator that the team cannot shape.

productThinkingTopics.question: How do you define an MVP without creating disposable architecture?
productThinkingTopics.coreAnswer: Minimize product scope, not correctness at critical boundaries. Keep data integrity, security, observability, accessibility, and clear contracts while deferring optional capabilities.
productThinkingTopics.example: Launch one reliable restaurant order workflow with a clear order model and instrumentation before adding kiosk variants, advanced analytics, and automation.
productThinkingTopics.commonMistake: Using MVP as permission for hidden data, security, or maintainability problems that block the next release.
